A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AutoVLA study and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and complete supplementary material. Renumbered and relocated content can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original driving experiments on NAVSIM, nuScenes, Waymo and CARLA, together with training ablations, runtime measurements and qualitative results.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds tokenization comparisons, codebook-size analyses and runtime measurements separated by thinking mode.

M1.justification: The Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone, 2048-token K-disk representation, dual-thinking supervised training and GRPO reinforcement fine-tuning remain unchanged. The new tokenization comparisons evaluate the existing design; revised sampling examples do not establish a new inference algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions retain nuPlan/NAVSIM, nuScenes, Waymo E2E, CARLA/Bench2Drive, DriveLM annotations and the WOMD codebook source. Added tokenization and runtime analyses probe the existing driving system without introducing a new dataset, driving task or input scenario.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 newly evaluates RT-1-style action binning and FAST (DCT) against K-disk tokenization; Table 6 adds a FAST planning comparison on NAVSIM. FAST was cited but not evaluated in v1. Existing driving-benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New tokenization experiments evaluate four codebook sizes using reconstruction ADE/FDE, movement coverage and codebook usage. Appendix E.4 replaces v1's specified temperature/top-p/top-k of 0.8/0.2/20 with illustrative slow-thinking settings of 1.0/0.5/20 and fast-thinking settings of 0.1/0.01/1. Their assignment to the revised benchmark results is unspecified; retained splits, training budgets and benchmark metrics are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a systematic investigation of a central component: Tables 4 and 6 compare tokenization alternatives, examine codebook-size sensitivity and connect representation quality to planning performance. Table 2 separately analyzes fast- and slow-thinking latency. These substantially extend v1's text-waypoint comparison and existing training ablations.

E5.justification: New Table 2 reports minimum and maximum runtimes alongside averages for each thinking mode, adding descriptive variability beyond v1's single runtime summaries. Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figure 4 and Table S2 revise nuScenes results and reverse important rankings: CoT/action-only UniAD average L2 changes from 0.86/0.70 m to 0.70/0.71 m, and collision averages from 0.35/0.31% to 0.31/0.35%. Text-waypoint PDMS changes from 59.24 in v1 Table 3 to 71.31 in v2 Table 5. New Tables 2, 4 and 6 add runtime and tokenization results, including FAST versus K-disk PDMS of 67.63 versus 80.54. The PDFs do not explain why the earlier scores changed.

T1.justification: The loss and GRPO equations, appendix KL and reward formulas, action-codebook construction and Algorithm 1 are retained. The new empirical analyses introduce no substantive mathematical definition, derivation, theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about unified reasoning and physical action generation, dual thinking, GRPO training and competitive driving performance. Added experiments support these existing contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 changes its nuScenes interpretation from reasoning being less useful in simple scenarios to reasoning benefiting from increased training data, although Appendix F.1 retains the previous explanation. Section 4.3 adds substantive explanations of tokenizer errors and the coverage-versus-redundancy rationale for 2048 tokens. New Appendix G discusses unsafe language instructions, adversarial threats and controlled deployment updates.

D1.justification: v2 describes the RT-1 comparator's acceleration/steering-rate bins and kinematic trajectory reconstruction. Appendix E.4 replaces one explicit decoding configuration with mode-specific examples, changing the reproducibility documentation without establishing which settings produced each result. Hardware, preprocessing, other training details and access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds the RT-1 reference and positions K-disk tokenization against RT-1-style binning and the previously cited FAST approach. The related-work section and other cited works remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: Editing is localized to the experimental discussion, expanded tokenization explanation and inference paragraph, plus terminology refinements, acknowledgements, a conference footer and Appendix G. The overall narrative and section organization remain stable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 2, 4 and 6, relocates NAVSIM Table 1 and Figure 4, and redraws Figure 4 with revised axis ranges and legend placement. Existing tables are renumbered or locally reformatted, while the architecture diagrams and qualitative appendix figures are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's text-waypoint comparison, v2's alternative-tokenizer and codebook-size studies provide stronger evidence for a central design choice, while Table 2 clarifies the latency tradeoff. These are useful but bounded gains. Their value is tempered by Appendix F.1 retaining an explanation inconsistent with the revised nuScenes discussion and Appendix E.4 no longer specifying one clear decoding configuration for the reported experiments.
